articles.title: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
articles.summary: A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’.
articles.body:
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.

“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.

In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.

Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.

Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.

Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.

A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.

By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.

The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.

Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.

The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.

The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.

Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.

A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.

According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.

Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.

Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.

Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.

In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.

July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.

By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.

Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.

Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.

These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.

Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.

Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.

By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.

Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.

Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.

In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.

The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.

The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.

Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.

Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.

Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.

A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.

Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.

In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.

Oxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.

A genocide finding requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Oxfam calls for full reparations where violations are established.

Its five-stage plan calls for securing access and reducing exposure, testing for contamination, screening sites and making essential repairs, treating contaminated sites and managing hazardous waste, then rebuilding with safeguards and long-term monitoring.

articles.title: At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
articles.summary: Mulitple strikes unleashed days after Putin promises a ‘painful’ response to Ukrainian attacks.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.

Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.

An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.

“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.

Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.

It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.

Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.

“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.

A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.

“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in nearby Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

Moscow has ramped up attacks on Ukraine and its energy network in particular as temperatures drop to around freezing.

Putin promised on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula, with “much more painful” attacks.

Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the part of it used by vehicles and halting train services.

Meanwhile, drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia’s Tatarstan region, damaging several, but there were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries, according to the Interfax news agency, which quoted local authorities.

“A fire broke out there,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova reported from Moscow, adding that the attack targeted the facility in Tatarstan’s Almetyevsk area.

Shapovalova said drone attacks were also reported in the Novoshakhtinsk area in Rostov, hitting a petroleum products plant and causing a fire in a storage tank.

She added that an attack was also reported in the city of Perm in the Volga region, where a large oil refinery is located.

Our correspondents said the attacks in Tatarstan, which is about 1,000km (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border, demonstrate Kyiv’s ability to penetrate deep inside Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine’s forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest ships, commissioned in 2023, near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.

Zelenskyy said they hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara. The Ukrainian president said it was used by Russia to transport weapons.

“We continue operations in designated waters,” he said on Telegram.

Zelenskyy added that a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette.

articles.title: Catering giant Compass Group to shift main stock market listing to US in further blow to UK
articles.summary: A growing number of firms have been leaving the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.
articles.body:
Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange.

A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday.

Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations.

It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times , is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic.

North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn.

However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.

These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter.

Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells.

'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

Action urged to halt exodus of firms leaving UK

The company was created during the Second World War after the Factories Canteen Order meant large manufacturing or munitions firms employing 250 people or more had an obligation to provide hot meals for workers.

Today, Compass operates across more than 25 countries and employs more than 600,000 people.

It is understood the group's proposed move to the US will have no impact on the number of UK employees and a consultation process with investors could take more than a year. It is expected to retain a secondary listing in London.

In a sign its listing could change, Compass changed the currency in which it trades its standard shares on the LSE from sterling to US dollars in April this year.

The boss of the LSE recently called on the government to do more to back homegrown companies and make the UK "more attractive" to invest in the domestic stock market.

Dame Julia Hoggett told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so.

Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

articles.title: SC directs West Bengal SIR tribunals to prioritise appeals challenging voter exclusion
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to give preference to pleas filed by voters challenging their exclusion from the electoral rolls, while deferring those contesting the inclusion of names.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the tribunals to separate appeals challenging voter exclusions from those contesting inclusions, and give priority to the exclusions.Also Read: West Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals"The second set of appeals (inclusion) does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred. The first set of appeals (exclusions) shall be given preference in the matter of final disposal," the bench said in its order, LiveLaw reported.The bench further directed the tribunals to prioritise, within the exclusion-related appeals, cases involving voters under the jurisdiction of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, given that civic body elections are due to be held soon.The Supreme Court also directed the Election Commission (EC) to increase the number of appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal SIR, in consultation with the chief justice of the Calcutta high court.Also Read: 93% of deleted Bengal voters have won appeals, EC tells SCThe top court was hearing petitions seeking steps to streamline and expedite the disposal of appeals before the tribunals set up to address grievances arising from SIR in the state.On August 25, the bench had directed the EC to submit details of pending and disposed-of appeals, with a separate count of cases filed by voters challenging their exclusion from or inclusion in the electoral rolls.The court had also asked the poll panel to specify how many additional tribunals would be needed to ensure that the appeals were decided within a stipulated timeframe.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Rough weather expected to hit both coasts, may disrupt Thanksgiving travel
articles.summary: Strong storms, serious flooding and powerful winds could dampen Thanksgiving travel plans and celebrations in parts of the Northeast and California, forecasters said.
articles.body: Strong storms, serious flooding and powerful winds could dampen Thanksgiving travel plans and celebrations in parts of the Northeast and California, forecasters said. A spinning winter cyclone developing Tuesday over the urban Northeast on Thanksgiving Day could create 50 mph wind gusts, boost coastal flooding, and produce “bursts of heavy rain and embedded thunderstorms,” the National Weather Service said. It described the storm as likely to quickly spool up and move fast due to “rapid cyclogenesis,” a term associated with rain-heavy storms known as bomb cyclones. The storms take place when air rises, barometric pressure drops and wind spirals. But the heaviest rain should hold off until the end of Thanksgiving Day. New York City Emergency Management is warning residents to stay tuned to weather alerts and forecasts this week. “Keep an eye on Thursday,” it said on X. “The forecast shows a storm that could bring strong winds, rain, and coastal flooding to the city on Thanksgiving Day, with gusts of 40 to 45 mph possible and 1 to 2 inches of rain.” It’s not clear how the weather might affect the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. New York City regulations state the parade’s hallmark balloons can’t fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph. Heavy rain, coastal flooding could hit East Coast The weather service’s hazardous weather outlooks for Wednesday and Thursday predict possible widespread and potentially heavy rain, strong winds, coastal flooding and high surf from southeast Virginia to waters off New Haven, Connecticut. The agency warns of winds 40 mph and stronger buffeting the Interstate 95 corridor in the Northeast midweek. “Confidence is increasing” that the system will produce serious weather after developing off the Southeast coast Wednesday and rapidly moving north, it said. Federal forecasters said the cyclone will spin and strengthen with the help of unusually warm Atlantic waters. The weather service added in a forecast discussion: “Coastal flooding issues, beach erosion, and dangerously rough seas appear likely, especially from the Mid-Atlantic up into the New England coast.” King tides and flooding in California Tuesday’s full moon will help pull seawater ashore on both U.S. coasts, with California officials preparing for the highest tides of the year and associated coastal flooding that could be exacerbated by an incoming Pacific storm. Coastal flood watches and advisories based on the year’s highest tides Tuesday through Thursday were in effect from Portland, Oregon, to the U.S.-Mexico border. The weather service said the winter pattern Pacific storm will move over land Tuesday in the Pacific Northwest and Northern California, with federal forecasters in San Francisco expecting 1 to 2 inches of rain through Wednesday, along with occasional 45 mph wind gusts. The Sierra Nevada will get fresh snow and pose “difficult travel,” the weather service office in Reno, Nevada, said. The West Coast storm is likely to be followed up by another, forecasters said, with those based in the San Francisco Bay Area saying it could strike Friday or over the weekend. Busy travel week Thanksgiving week’s departure and arrival days often vie for the title of the busiest travel day in America, with Transportation Safety Administration data showing Nov. 30, 2025, with the most daily airport security screenings, more than 3.1 million, for the year. This year, Tuesday is proving to be the best day to travel to Thanksgiving locations, either by air or road, before the Northeast storms wreak havoc later in the week. On Wednesday, those heading to the airport from Miami to Charlotte could face weather-related issues. Motor Club AAA said slightly fewer travelers are expected on highways and in the air during the typically busy Thanksgiving travel period. A post-pandemic streak of an increasing number of travelers during Thanksgiving week each year is likely to come to an end as slightly fewer people, 81.5 million, leave home for holiday trips compared to 81.6 million last year, AAA said in a statement. The week’s travelers are contending with higher prices for gas and airfare, with roundtrip tickets up 17% over Thanksgiving 2025, and the average price at $800, it said. Gas station price app GasBuddy projects the national average for a gallon of gas to be $3.62 Thursday, a likely record high for the date but also reflective of prices falling rapidly — by at least .50 cents — so far this month.

articles.title: Don Toliver concert evacuated in U.K. after ‘unknown substance’ released in crowd
articles.summary: MANCHESTER, England — Thousands of people attending a concert of American rapper Don Toliver were evacuated from a major British arena Sunday evening, police said, after an “unknown substance” was released into the crowd.
articles.body: MANCHESTER, England — Thousands of people attending a concert of American rapper Don Toliver were evacuated from a major British arena Sunday evening, police said, after an “unknown substance” was released into the crowd. About 12,000 concertgoers were evacuated by emergency workers just after 10 p.m. local time (5 p.m. ET) from Toliver’s show at the Co-op Live venue in the northern English city of Manchester. The North West Ambulance Service declared a major incident and​ said the substance was “believed to ​be tear gas” and was understood to ⁠have been released toward the ​end of the show. “We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene,” it said in a statement, adding that one person had been hospitalized. “More than 80 people were assessed by our clinicians, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination was carried out as a precaution,” the ambulance service said Monday. People in the crowd were suffering effects “from an unknown substance,” Greater Manchester police said in its latest statement Monday. “Enquiries are underway into what the substance is and what caused the incident,” police added. The venue, in the center of the busy city, was hosting Grammy Award-nominated R&B rapper-singer Toliver, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, as part of his Nitrous tour. The Houston-based rapper is best known for hits “No idea” and “After Party,” and features on the soundtrack to the new “Grand Theft Auto VI” blockbuster game. Toliver has yet to publicly comment on the incident but is due to perform in London on Monday and Tuesday as part of his tour. Manchester was left shaken in 2017 after a bombing at a nearby venue during an Ariana Grande concert left 22 people dead and made global headlines. “We understand the concern that this incident will have raised,” Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said Monday. “We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about.” “Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital,” Parker added. Concertgoer Joey Howe, 22, told BBC Radio Manchester the lights came on and Toliver appeared to have been “rushed off stage.” “I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue,” Howe said. He said people were “choking” and there was a “horrible smell” in the arena. “It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see,” he added. Another fan, Ben Stevenson, told the Manchester Evening News that he was in the standing section of the arena when he “started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy.” A spokesman for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a former mayor of Manchester, called the incident “deeply worrying” and said the police would conduct a full investigation. The venue, which opened in 2024, is due to host American singer Phoebe Bridgers on Thursday. It said in a statement on X that it was “working closely with Greater Manchester Police to identify the cause and action appropriately. Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update.”

articles.title: New owner for Acorn carbon capture and storage project in Aberdeenshire
articles.summary: Greek company EnEarth has now taken a 30% share in the Aberdeenshire project.
articles.body:
The Acorn carbon capture and storage project in Aberdeenshire has a new owner after the main developer put its stake up for sale.

The project will take carbon dioxide emissions from industrial processes in Scotland and store them in depleted gas reservoirs under the North Sea via the terminal at St Fergus.

Concerns had been raised about the viability of the Acorn Project after major stakeholder Storegga said it planned to sell its share.

The Greek company EnEarth has now taken a 30% share, and becomes the lead developer.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

The Acorn project aims to decarbonise Scotland's high polluting industrial sites by capturing and transporting emissions using redundant underground gas pipes.

Focus had long been on Grangemouth and Mossmorran as the two main sites for capturing that carbon dioxide.

A new gas-fired power station at Peterhead, which was given the go-ahead last month , will be built so emissions can be captured and stored as part of the Acorn project.

The influential Climate Change Committee has said that carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) is a vital component in the drive to decarbonise the UK by the middle of the century.

Some environmental groups, like Friends of the Earth Scotland, have long argued that it is unproven technology which acts only as a mechanism for the oil and gas industry to continue business as normal.

For businesses in north east Scotland, where oil and gas production peaked 25 years ago, low carbon technologies are seen as vital for ensuring an energy transition does not create industrial wastelands.

New owner EnEarth said it was committed to the venture in Aberdeenshire.

"Acorn is a project of strategic importance to Scotland's industrial decarbonisation and the wider European energy transition," chief executive officer Nikolas Rigas said.

"Building on our experience developing transport and storage infrastructure in Greece and Bulgaria, we are committed to accelerating Acorn's development and unlocking its full potential.

"We look forward to working closely with our partners, governments and local communities to deliver this critical infrastructure, support industrial competitiveness, attract investment and create long-term skilled jobs."

The UK government's Minister for Local Energy and Jobs Martin McCluskey described it as an "important step forward" for the project.

"Acorn has the potential to create thousands of good, skilled jobs, back British industry and put Scotland at the forefront of carbon capture," he said.

"We look forward to seeing the new plans for the project that the new owners will bring to the table to put Acorn on a strong footing."

articles.title: Marilyn Monroe's 1950s stuffing recipe fetched $16,000 at auction — and holds clue to Joe DiMaggio marriage
articles.summary: A handwritten Thanksgiving stuffing recipe from Marilyn Monroe, with 18 ingredients and a "No garlic" note, sold for $16,000 and fuels Joe DiMaggio speculation.
articles.body: A Thanksgiving recipe of Marilyn Monroe's was just as fabulous as she was and offers a glimpse into a lesser-known side of the Hollywood star. Her handwritten stuffing recipe is a far cry from the boxed bread-and-herb side many families serve on Thanksgiving, loaded with 18 ingredients including sourdough, ground beef, poultry livers or hearts, hard-boiled eggs, raisins, Parmesan and nuts. Written in pencil on both sides of a sheet of City Title Insurance Company stationery, the recipe was cataloged by Julien's Auctions as circa 1954. It sold for $16,000 at the auction house's June 2026 sale, more than five times its estimate. JESSIE JAMES DECKER SHARES 'SECRET SAUCE' BEHIND FAMILY'S FOOD, FAITH, TRADITIONS The recipe is attributed to Monroe because it is written entirely in her hand, according to Julien's Auctions, and came from the estate of her acting coach, Lee Strasberg, who inherited her personal effects. "Something as simple as a handwritten recipe helps humanize Marilyn and reminds us that behind one of the most recognizable faces in Hollywood history was a woman who enjoyed many of the same ordinary pleasures as everyone else," Scott Fortner, a lifelong Monroe scholar and collector who is often consulted on authenticating her personal effects, told Fox News Digital. "I think it offers a wonderful glimpse into another side of Marilyn Monroe, beyond the glamorous movie star and Hollywood sex symbol," he added, noting that she had "a genuine interest in cooking and domestic life." She reportedly enjoyed cooking and entertaining, especially during her later marriage to playwright Arthur Miller when the couple had a farm in Connecticut. 'FOOD BABE' DECLARES WAR ON THE 'HOLIDAY DEATH AISLE' AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING "Her personal library also included several cookbooks, some with markings and annotations," Fortner said. The San Francisco address on the stationery and the note "No garlic" have fueled speculation about a connection to baseball legend Joe DiMaggio, who reportedly disliked garlic and with whom Monroe lived in San Francisco after their 1954 marriage. Fortner said it is possible she made the stuffing for the former Yankees star, but there is no documented evidence of that. CLASSIC AMERICAN PANTRY STAPLES ARE GETTING A MAJOR PROTEIN- AND FIBER-PACKED MAKEOVER He said the San Francisco stationery makes it reasonable to think Monroe wrote the recipe during her relationship with Joe DiMaggio, whom she began dating in 1952 and married in January 1954, but the timing remains unclear. The couple separated in October, so if Monroe wrote it later that year, they would have been apart by Thanksgiving, Fortner noted. The sourdough, he added, could reflect San Francisco's food culture, but it is also a common stuffing ingredient. "Just because the recipe was written on stationery from a San Francisco business doesn't necessarily mean it was written while Marilyn was in San Francisco, or even during her relationship with Joe," Fortner told Fox News Digital. "Without knowing exactly when she wrote the recipe, we can only speculate about its connection to Joe or whether she ever prepared the dish for him." 6 VINTAGE RECIPES OF DECADES PAST, FROM OYSTER STUFFING TO HOT DR PEPPER Regardless, the relic reminds us that Monroe "valued her personal relationships and had a genuine interest in the everyday experiences of life outside the movie studio," Fortner said. For home cooks hoping to bring a bit of Monroe's kitchen to their own Thanksgiving table, The New York Times published a modern adaptation of the recipe that could feed a crowd. It yields nearly 20 cups and follows Monroe's handwritten instructions to use sourdough soaked in cold water instead of broth. Her note suggests the stuffing for chicken, turkey or even pheasant. Below is an adaptation of Monroe's recipe. articles.title: Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
articles.summary: Drone strikes on two Russian vessels near Libyan coast fuels fears of Ukraine war’s spread.
articles.body:
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.

“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.

The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.

The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.

The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.

The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.

Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.

Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.

“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.

A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.

In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.

Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.

Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Ukraine’s attacks off the coast of Libya, as well as the targeting of Russian cargo vessels in the Baltic Sea, as a “very dangerous trend”.

Peskov warned Ukraine of “painful” consequences. “The Defence Ministry is dealing with this matter, and information will also be provided through the Defence Ministry if deemed appropriate,” he said.

Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.

“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.

“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.

The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.

On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.

“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.

The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.

How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?

At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.

The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.

In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.

In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.

Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?

Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.

“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.

He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.

Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.

“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.

The sinking of the Merkury, commissioned in 2023, would also weaken Russia’s naval capabilities, Muraviev said.

However, the academic warned that the Gulf of Finland was particularly sensitive because of its geography and the proximity of Russian and NATO forces.

“In my personal view, it is an area where a possible clash between Russia and NATO is quite possible,” he said.

Muraviev added that the attacks could have wider implications for global shipping, which is already facing heightened security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.

“[The attacks] just add additional risks to marine operators from across the world,” he said.

articles.title: Kerala: Police investigate fairness cream's alleged link to kidney ailment in 17-year-old Indian girl
articles.summary: Doctors who treated the 17-year-old girl say that the cream allegedly contained toxic levels of mercury.
articles.body:
Police in India's southern Kerala state have registered a case against a fairness cream brand after a 17-year-old girl who used the cream allegedly developed a serious kidney ailment.

The girl's doctor told the media that she had developed a disease that impairs the kidney's ability to filter blood due to toxic levels of mercury allegedly found in the cream.

The girl - her name has been withheld to protect her identity - reportedly bought the cream to treat pimples and pigmentation after seeing an ad on social media.

India has an obsession with skin-lightening creams and this has led to a proliferation of brands selling fairness creams, though not all of them are regulated.

Experts say some of these creams may contain toxic metals like mercury and lead, but because they are sold via WhatsApp and other social media platforms, the brands often escape scrutiny of the authorities.

They also say that many of these brands use social media to market products to youngsters, even if they are uncertified and untested.

Laboratory tests revealed that the cream the girl used contained 12,500 parts per million of mercury, far exceeding the permissible limit of less than one part per million for skin-lightening products, Aster MIMS Mother Hospital in Malappuram district, where the teenager was treated, said in a statement.

Dr Satheesh, a nephrologist at the hospital, said that the girl had developed membranous nephropathy - a life-threatening kidney disorder where immune deposits thicken the filtering walls of the kidneys, causing large amounts of protein to leak into the urine.

She added that mercury absorbed through the skin could damage the kidneys' filtration units, leading to blood toxicity. If left untreated, such toxicity could cause kidney failure and severe neurological damage.

The girl said she started buying the fairness cream about a year ago through a social media app and had bought three bottles over the past year.

"The company claimed that continuous use [of the cream] every night would help remove pimples and pigmentation. It also promised visible results with consistent application," the teenager told Onmanorama newspaper.

But after using the cream for a couple of months, she began experiencing fatigue, headaches, dizziness, insomnia and her legs and face began to swell. The teenager told the newspaper that she even struggled to stand upright.

"The teenager was initially brought to the hospital by her parents with severe body swelling and acute physical distress," the hospital said.

"While primary treatment was initiated, the unusual progression of her symptoms prompted doctors to suspect an underlying toxin. Subsequent blood and clinical tests revealed dangerously elevated levels of mercury in her system," their statement added.

Doctors suspected that the mercury could have entered the girl's bloodstream through her skin. They sent a sample of the fairness cream to a laboratory for testing.

The test results confirmed that the cream contained mercury "drastically higher than" the permissible safety limits mandated by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) for cosmetics in India, the hospital said.

The doctors then treated the girl by administering medicines to eliminate toxins, while managing her kidney-related complications.

She was discharged from hospital after about a month and has been recovering at home.

On Monday, she told the BBC that she was still experiencing some health issues and was finding it difficult to study.

"Since starting treatment, she has shown gradual improvement. However, she is not back to normal yet and it may still take time for her to fully recover," Dr Satheesh said.

Meanwhile, the Kerala police have launched an investigation into the matter and the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has also registered a case against the fairness cream manufacturer.

The incident once again puts the spotlight on India's obsession with fair skin, and how people, especially women, are willing to buy creams that may not be regulated as long as they promise to make them fair.

This is because the cultural bias against dark skin runs deep in Indian society and those who aren't fair-skinned often face discrimination.

In recent years, social activists and even Bollywood actors have spoken out about this unhealthy preference for fair skin, challenging the widely-held notion that fairer is better.

articles.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
articles.body:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says .

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."

"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.

Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.

"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.summary: Democrats in the South look to 2027 governor’s races. Extreme weather could disrupt Thanksgiving plans. And the Army’s detonation in Iowa.
articles.body: Democrats in the South hope to capitalize on the blue wave momentum. Extreme weather on both coasts could disrupt Thanksgiving plans. And the arrest of a father and daughter by masked ICE officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle sparks a backlash. Here’s what to know today. Democrats look to 2027 races for governor to build on gains in the South Democrats calling on their party to invest in the South after historic victories this year won’t have to wait until 2028, with races for governor in Mississippi, Louisiana and Kentucky ahead in 2027. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. “As a Southern Democrat, we were often overlooked, underfunded, sometimes even looked down upon,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chaired the Democratic Governors Association this year, told NBC News. “But we have scrapped our way back to the table.” Beshear is part of a chorus of party members who think the region could be cemented as a competitive battleground. Meghan Meehan-Draper, the DGA’s executive director, said they’ll be capitalizing on post-midterms energy into the upcoming elections. “I hope that these recent wins in 2026 show everyone that, again, no state is off the map,” she said. Read about the prospective candidates in each race. The party is also planning for 2028: The Democratic National Committee announced that it’ll hold a dozen presidential debates starting next June, using criteria like polling and grassroots fundraising to determine eligibility. Rough weather expected to hit both coasts on Thanksgiving Strong storms, serious flooding and powerful winds could dampen Thanksgiving travel plans and celebrations on both coasts, forecasters said. A spinning winter cyclone over the urban Northeast on Thursday could create 50 mph wind gusts, boost coastal flooding and produce “bursts of heavy rain and embedded thunderstorms,” the National Weather Service said. It described the storm as likely to quickly spool up and move fast due to “rapid cyclogenesis,” a term associated with rain-heavy storms known as bomb cyclones. The storms take place when air rises, barometric pressure drops, and wind spirals. New York City Emergency Management also warned residents of extreme weather, though it was unclear how it might affect the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Meanwhile, California officials are preparing for the highest tides of the year and associated coastal flooding that could be exacerbated by an incoming Pacific storm. Advisories were in effect from Portland, Oregon to the U.S.-Mexico border. Here’s what else to know. Elsewhere, over 1,000 Delta flights were delayed Sunday after an automated system that calculates an aircraft’s weight malfunctioned during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. ICE arrest of father and daughter boarding Seattle flight sparks backlash A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday. Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday filmed the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The videos were widely seen on social media. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed. Read the full story here. Ukraine sinks Russian warship off Libya in latest expansion of the war Ukraine has taken its fight against Russia to the shores of North Africa, claiming to have sunk a Russian warship near the Libyan port of Benghazi in its latest bold expansion of the war, just a day after Moscow said another of its ships was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukrainian naval drones had been used in the attack in the Mediterranean. He shared footage showing drones approaching several vessels followed by massive fire balls. The escalation in the international waters comes just days after the much-touted three-way gathering between the leaders of Russia, China and the U.S., during which President Donald Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend.” Read the full story here. Staff Pick: How a rocket scientist is fueling the NFL’s best defense When we heard that the Minnesota Vikings hired a former rocket scientist to their coaching staff, we thought it might just be another data cruncher applying sophisticated analytics to the game. As we learned more about his journey to the gridiron, we realized this wasn’t just a story about football and numbers. It’s about perseverance, determination and chasing your dreams. Chenzo Funari ascended to great heights in aerospace, helping produce SpaceX’s famed Raptor engines. But even with all his success, he told us he didn’t feel fulfilled. Funari’s first and one true love was football, which he played until injuries in high school sidelined him for good. Determined to get back into the game, Funari quit his job to volunteer as a coach for the Youngstown State Football team. He worked his way through multiple collegiate football programs, and finally got on the radar of the Vikings. We traveled to the team’s Minnesota facilities to speak to Funari and the staff he works with. Coaches and players alike were impressed by his ability to process information differently than others in the building, as well as his drive to come up with unique play calls. And even though he didn’t take the traditional route of most NFL coaches, everyone in the building kept telling us the same thing: Funari’s mind was made for football. articles.title: Next data accessed in cyber breach
articles.summary: The fashion retailer says there is no evidence customers' personal data was compromised.
articles.body:
Next has said that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier.

The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.

The firm - which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire - said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".

"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.

"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.

"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."

The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness", and working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.

Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.

In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account , leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.

The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.

In 2025 Marks & Spencer suffered from a major cyber-attack, which forced it to stop all online sales for about six weeks and led to some empty shelves in shops.

articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video of Ukraine's naval drones sinking Russia's corvette Merkury off Libya, as peace talks resume after a nine-month pause.
articles.body: The war between Russia and Ukraine continues to spill outside the countries' boundaries, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared a video of a drone striking and sinking Russian weapons ships off the coast of Libya. "We continue our operations in designated waters," Zelenskyy wrote early Monday morning in a statement on X. "We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukraine weapons. Glory to Ukraine!" The strikes come as President Donald Trump is pushing for peace, but Ukraine has remained steadfast in not only fighting off Russian gains in south and east of Ukraine, but also taking the fight to Russia "in designated waters" around the globe. RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war," the post began. "I thank the warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine and all our Defense Forces of Ukraine who took part in carrying out these tasks. I received detailed briefings on the operation’s steps yesterday and today – the targets we set were achieved. It all took place off the coast of Libya. "Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It’s one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war. A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette. Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit." UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Sunday's drone strike hit the Russian vessel while it was docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya – a region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army maintains ties with Russia. The Institute for the Study of War reported that the Merkury had stopped at Benghazi for several days under a cooperation agreement to refuel and resupply while escorting Russian cargo vessels capable of carrying military supplies back to Russia. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the Baltic Sea incident part of a "dangerous trend of increasing terrorist activity" and urged regional nations to warn Kyiv against such operations. Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels fought the blaze after the Sparta II drifted into Finnish waters before a Russian vessel began towing it away Sunday. UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS Osama Hamad, prime minister of Libya's eastern-based government, said he asked the United Nations to investigate "suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya" and to verify whether Ukrainian military experts are operating there. Western Libya is governed by the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli, which did not immediately respond to requests for comment. UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA The Benghazi operation follows earlier maritime incidents far outside the Black Sea theater. UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL' The expanding naval strikes come as U.S.-backed peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv resumed this month after a nine-month pause. The sticking point remains Russian annexation of occupied Ukrainian in exchange for potential NATO-like security guarantees. Zelenskyy had told Fox News of some potential negotiation of land for security, but has since balked at giving up on the land bridge sought by Vladimir Putin to connect Russia to the Black Sea. The overland route connecting Russia to the Black Sea coast and Crimea runs through occupied southern Ukraine – specifically the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions – alongside the 19-kilometer (12-mile) Crimean Bridge across the Kerch Strait. UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA Ukraine strategically struck the Crimean Bridge while Trump was getting ready to meet with Putin and China's Xi Jinping. The meeting came thereafter and did not result in any movements toward peace. Mykola Bielieskov of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv told Reuters that Ukraine is seeking leverage through "horizontal escalation." articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: NIH funded foreign labs with troubling safety lapses, including deadly bat virus experiment
articles.summary: PETA alleges the National Institutes of Health funded foreign animal labs with biosafety failures, including a halted Hendra virus bat study in Australia.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded millions of taxpayer dollars to foreign animal research facilities where significant biosafety, containment and staffing failures allegedly took place — including a bat virus experiment in Australia that was abruptly halted after animal containment broke down, according to federal records obtained by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) and reviewed by Fox News Digital. The internal agency records and noncompliance reports show that federal health officials repeatedly approved funding or failed to identify major safety and oversight vulnerabilities until after taxpayer-funded animal experiments were already underway. In response to the findings, PETA on Monday sent a formal complaint to NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, demanding that the agency immediately halt all federal funding for animal experiments conducted outside the U.S. The newly released information comes amid mounting scrutiny on Capitol Hill regarding foreign research oversight and renewed calls for the bipartisan Cease Animal Research Grants Overseas (CARGO) Act, which would permanently prohibit NIH from bankrolling animal experiments in foreign countries. GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION Deadly bat virus experiment halted over biosafety lapses According to federal documents, the NIH funded a study on Hendra virus — a lethal, bat-borne pathogen — at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness, operated by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO. The project, "Shining a light on bat cellular immunity following virus infection," was suspended by the facility’s Animal Ethics Committee after serious operational failures surfaced. Internal records show the facility suffered from insufficient appropriately trained personnel capable of conducting animal procedures at the required biocontainment level, an absence of adequate contingency planning, unclear protocols and prolonged confinement of flying foxes without proper enrichment. RIDGLAN FARMS BEAGLES BEGIN LEAVING WISCONSIN FACILITY AFTER RESCUE GROUPS STRIKE DEAL FOR RELEASE After a single flying fox tested positive for Hendra virus, staff were forced to kill all eight bats housed together because the room could not be elevated to Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) containment. A ninth flying fox housed separately at BSL-4 was later killed after also testing positive. The primary investigator alerted the NIH to the infections in May 2023, leading the ethics board to suspend the study weeks later. However, the NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) did not receive even a preliminary report of the suspension until April 2024 — more than 10 months after the shutdown, according to records. The documents show the Australian bat study was not an isolated incident. At Newcastle University in the United Kingdom, where researchers conducted NIH-funded brain and stroke research on nonhuman primates, a 2025 federal review ordered the facility to reevaluate its personal protective equipment standards, tuberculosis screening and emergency procedures for testing potential human exposures to the deadly Herpes B virus. 'Enhanced' inspections run on institution-controlled cameras Following past international scandals — including a shuttered Colombian facility that received $17 million in U.S. funding while keeping monkeys in squalor — the NIH pledged to implement "enhanced oversight" of foreign institutions in line with Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendations. However, PETA’s review of 124 federal files obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) shows the NIH’s oversight relies almost entirely on self-reporting and scripted virtual site visits. Records show that virtual visits were announced months in advance, allowing overseas facilities ample time to prepare. At Newcastle University, the facility received notice in May 2025 for a virtual visit that did not happen until December. Notification letters outlined prearranged planning sessions, document reviews and camera tours where foreign personnel controlled what government monitors could see on screen. The format gave federal regulators no ability to conduct unannounced walk-throughs, inspect arbitrary rooms, review records in real time or conduct confidential staff interviews, according to records. Out of 70 annual reports examined regarding active NIH-backed animal research across foreign labs between 2023 and 2025, 67 self-reported zero violations, reflecting a system almost entirely dependent on foreign labs self-policing their own programs. HARVARD-CHINA LINKS UNEARTHED AS CONGRESS FINDS 140 PAPERS CO-AUTHORED BY CCP MILITARY UNIVERSITIES Unapproved labs, unaccounted animals and missing assurances The records also document widespread administrative failures, including grants flowing to institutions that lacked basic federal authorization: The NIH awarded a $13 million tuberculosis vaccine adjuvant contract to the University of Sydney in 2022, but the animal testing was outsourced to the Centenary Institute in Australia, an entity lacking the required NIH Foreign Animal Welfare Assurance. The unauthorized setup went unnoticed by the NIH for years until the university inquired about the death of an experimental mouse in 2025. HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY The NIH also confirmed that it could find "no records of an assurance" for multiple foreign entities carrying out U.S.-funded animal studies, including Australian biotech firm Kinoxis Therapeutics, which conducted opioid withdrawal experiments on 80 dogs, 314 rats and 1,485 mice under a grant active through May 2026. Similar record absences occurred for grants involving animal testing at institutions in Canada, Kenya and Israel. At the Research Center in Clinical Biochemistry and Immunology in Argentina, the NIH funded a multi-year Chagas disease study. A 2026 preprint co-authored by the lead researcher detailed mice experiencing continuous whole-body tremors and hind-limb paralysis — conditions mandating euthanasia under the approved protocol. However, the lab reported that untreated animals died over an extended 120-day timeframe and admitted it does not generate animal monitoring or veterinary records, leaving federal regulators with no documentation of how animal deaths were tracked. WHITE HOUSE REBUKES CBS INTERVIEW AFTER HOST BATTLES NIH DIRECTOR OVER LOSS OF TRUST IN PUBLIC HEALTH PETA, lawmakers call to cut off overseas animal lab funding In her letter Monday to Bhattacharya, Dr. Magnolia Martínez, PETA’s lead projects manager and congressional liaison, argued that the NIH's foreign monitoring regime is fundamentally broken. The organization noted that an Animal Welfare Assurance represents a baseline administrative requirement that does not ensure animal welfare or clinical applicability to human health, urging the agency to halt funding foreign animal tests and redirect resources toward human-biology-based research methods. Fox News Digital reached out to the NIH for comment on the reported biosafety lapses, the oversight timeline and calls to halt overseas animal grants, but did not immediately receive a response. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lawmakers in Washington are similarly ramping up efforts to cut off foreign funding through the CARGO Act, emphasizing that American taxpayers should not be underwriting unaccountable and hazardous research in foreign jurisdictions. Fox News Digital reached out to bipartisan sponsors of the CARGO Act — including Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Dina Titus, D-Nev. — asking whether the newly revealed foreign laboratory failures will prompt renewed legislative action and oversight hearings to permanently ban federal funding for overseas animal experiments.

articles.title: Mystery of unknown skeleton buried at Westminster Abbey may finally be solved after 150 years
articles.summary: A skeleton unearthed at Westminster Abbey in 1869 puzzled experts for 150 years, until new research linked the bones to two high-ranking medieval monks.
articles.body: An archaeologist may have finally solved the mystery of the unknown skeleton buried on the grounds of Westminster Abbey, one of London's most popular tourist sites — and the answer points to a 1,000-year-old recycling job. The research centers on an unidentified skeleton that was found at Westminster Abbey in 1869, according to news agency SWNS. The skeleton was found inside a Roman limestone sarcophagus bearing an inscription for Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy 4th-century Briton — but the remains inside don't belong to him. STARTLING MYSTERY REVEALED IN CENTURIES-OLD ROYAL TOMBS AT POWERFUL QUEEN'S MONASTERY When the skeleton was excavated at Westminster Abbey in 1869, archaeologists noticed that a distinctive early medieval Latin cross was sculpted on the lid. The symbol puzzled experts for over 150 years because it didn't match the Roman-era casket. The recent study, published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, was led by Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey, SWNS said. Rodwell's work followed a 2025 excavation of the Abbey's vestry, which was required ahead of construction on the new King Charles III Sacristy set to open in 2027. 'DIG OF THE CENTURY' BENEATH NOTRE DAME REVEALS MYSTERIOUS MARKINGS, ANCIENT SECRETS In the study, Rodwell argues the skeleton may belong to one of two high-ranking medieval monks who died in the 11th century. The two candidates are monks named Aelfwig, who died around 1020, and his successor Wulnoth, who died in 1049. Carbon dating placed the bones between 987 and 1052 A.D., which lines up with both individuals' lifetimes. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We do not know the date of birth of either," Rodwell said, as SWNS noted. "But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died." Another clue, Rodwell said, was that the occupant was honored with a "fine" sarcophagus — even if it was recycled. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The man was likely between 35 and 49 years old when he died, and stood 5 feet, 9 inches tall. Researchers also found white lime residue inside the stone casket outlining where a wooden coffin had once sat before decaying over the centuries. The sarcophagus is currently on display at Westminster Abbey in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The discovery is one of many recent skeletal finds across England that have shed light on the country's medieval past. In 2025, archaeologists excavating a former department store site at the University of Gloucestershire uncovered 317 skeletons and the ruins of a medieval church. articles.title: Iran says it will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
articles.summary: Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Iran will use all tools to confront the naval siege and defend itself.
articles.body:
Iran says it will use all means at its disposal to counter a United States naval blockade imposed during the nine-month US-Israel war on Iran.

The ⁠US blockade was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached ⁠a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.

“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news briefing on Monday.

“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitute an act of military aggression against Iran,” Baghaei said.

“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”

The war broke out on February 28 when the US and Israel carried out air strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.

The conflict has since expanded after Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the region and with armed groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.

The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict with Iran continuing in its efforts to block the waterway, which is vital for oil and natural gas shipments.

In an attempt to force Iran to halt efforts to block the strait, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and later announced a series of economic sanctions and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.

Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks that ships have caught fire while trying to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.

TankerTrackers.com said last week that a tanker was loading Iranian crude oil in the Gulf via ship-to-ship transfer and could become the first vessel to successfully export the country’s crude since the US reimposed the blockade in July.

Baghaei said on Monday that reports about Iranian ships loading oil are “speculation”.

Visible Iranian crude exports decreased to near zero in recent months due to the blockade.

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the US blockade is hurting Iran economically.

“Iranians are aware of that and they are publicly admitting it because more than 80 percent of the country’s imports and exports happen through the Strait of Hormuz or southern ports of the country,” he said.

“Iranians are now looking increasingly for options to put an end to the US naval blockade,” our correspondent said, adding that military action against US military assets around Iran is being discussed.

“Escalation is now the main option on the table,” he said.

Diplomatic efforts to resolve the war remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June agreement that laid out a path to a permanent settlement.

Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days if Washington meets its conditions, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions.

“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” Baghaei said.
